doc_summary: Buck Shlegeris asks why Redwood's empirical safety research has sped up only about 2-3x with AI when METR and Anthropic estimates imply roughly 5-10x uplift. He weighs scaffold, task-type and judgment-bottleneck explanations, and predicts that third-party output will soon show whether the speedup is real. The post is not about eval realism, so the items are indirect and capture his evidence standards.

items.claim: prefers consistency across independent estimates over a single opaque self-reported number because an unclear methodology makes a surprising claim hard to trust.
items.quote: I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising

items.claim: Updates on a surprising claim only when a separate line of evidence converges on it, rather than on the claim's own assertion.
items.quote: but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report

items.claim: prefers observable output rates (published results) over subjective impressions of speedup because the true effect should show up in concrete deliverables.
items.quote: If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon.

items.claim: Tests a hypothesis on the cases most favourable to it, since failure there is the most informative result.
items.quote: At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong.

items.claim: Distrusts autonomous-agent research outputs because the model makes bad judgment calls that invalidate results, so outputs need checking before being believed.
items.quote: Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings

items.claim: When a result is surprising, enumerates competing explanations (adoption failure, task mix, management bottleneck) and then judges which is the real cause from direct experience.
items.quote: It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us.

items.claim: Attributes gaps in measured effect to task suitability, noting that some projects are much more amenable to agent use than others.
items.quote: this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows.

items.claim: Uses market logic as a sanity check: if a scaffold were drastically better, the lab would have productised it.
items.quote: If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products?

items.claim: Treats research speed as bottlenecked by judgment and management time rather than raw labor once AI labor gets cheap.
items.quote: Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed?
